No, not on what this tool can find. Your lease says the amenity fee "is not refundable for any reason, including the closure of any amenity" (Lease Section 3.3), and that a closure does not entitle you to "any refund of the amenity fee" (Lease Section 6.2).

The statute text I have has nothing on amenities or amenity fees; the search found no match. The one part II section that can override a lease term here is Fla. Stat. 83.47(1): a term is void to the extent it waives a right or remedy in this part, or limits a landlord's liability "arising under law". That helps you only if part II gives you a right to this refund, and the tool found no section that does. You confirmed the problem is not the structure or plumbing that 83.51(1)(b) names.

Lease Section 6.2 also lets the landlord close an amenity "for maintenance, repair, weather, or safety, for as long as Landlord reasonably determines." You confirmed the pool has been closed since you moved in, for resurfacing. Whether that length of closure is reasonable is not something the lease text or the statute text settles.

Two cases are on clauses of this kind, both about injuries, not fees. Fuentes v. Owen, 310 So. 2d 458, read a lease clause releasing the landlord from claims for damage to persons or property, and said such clauses are enforceable only where the intent is "clear and unequivocal" (at 459). Your clause says "for any reason, including the closure of any amenity", which is plain, so that cuts against you. Ray v. Tampa Windridge Associates, 596 So. 2d 676, which read 83.51(2)(a) as it stood in 1985, said provisions that excuse a landlord from a part II duty are "prohibited by section 83.47" (at 678). It would help you only if part II made the landlord owe you working amenities, and the tool found no section that says so. Neither case is about a fee or an amenity, so how far either reaches you is not settled.

A refund claim that rests on other Florida law, such as how the ads were worded, is outside this tool.

On the fee, yes, the tool still finds no basis for a refund. But a lease cannot take away every right. A lease term is "void and unenforceable to the extent that it" waives or precludes the rights, remedies, or requirements in part II (Fla. Stat. 83.47(1)(a)). So the lines saying no "any reduction or abatement of Rent" (Lease Section 5.2) and no "any reduction of Rent" (Lease Section 6.2) cannot take away a part II rent remedy that applies to you. That only protects rights part II gives, and the tool found none for a refund of the amenity fee.

Whether a part II remedy applies to you is not known yet. Ending the lease (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)) turns on whether the landlord had a duty to fix this: your lease says it repairs this kind of problem, which the sheet asks you, or a local building, housing, or health code requires it, which the city or county code enforcement office can tell you. Not paying rent as a defense (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)) turns only on a local code, because you confirmed the problem is not the structure or plumbing.

Whether the ads count is outside this tool. It holds only ch. 83 part II, and the search for "advertis" in the statute found nothing. The tool found nothing on ads in your lease's text either, after several wordings, including "advertis", "marketing", "promise", and "entire agreement".

What your lease does say about these things stands apart from the ads. It lets you use the "swimming pool, fitness center, study rooms, and clubhouse", subject to the community rules and posted hours (Lease Section 6.1), and says rent includes "high-speed internet (Wi-Fi)" (Lease Section 5.1). It also lets the landlord close an amenity (Lease Section 6.2) and says the landlord is not liable for outages "caused by a provider" (Lease Section 5.2). You confirmed the landlord only answers "the provider is aware"; whether the Wi-Fi drops were in fact caused by a provider, the tool does not know. Whether 83.47(1)(b), which voids terms that limit a landlord's liability "arising under law", reaches a claim built on the ads is outside the tool.

A rent credit is not an option the tool tracks on its own. The closest part II rule applies when a failure is "due to causes beyond the control of the landlord and the landlord has made and continues to make every reasonable effort to correct the failure to comply" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)). Then, if the unit stays livable and you stay in it, "the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)(b)).

Whether that is open to you is not known yet. It turns on these points:

- Whether the Wi-Fi counts. Your lease says rent includes "high-speed internet (Wi-Fi)" (Lease Section 5.1), and 83.56(1) reaches "material provisions of the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)). The statute does not settle what "material" means. On one reading it turns on degree: how serious the failure is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living in the unit. On the other, materiality comes from a duty 83.51(1) lists, and you confirmed this problem is not the structure or plumbing.
- The cause. Your lease says the landlord is not liable for outages "caused by a provider" (Lease Section 5.2). You confirmed the landlord only answers "the provider is aware". Whether the drops are beyond the landlord's control, and whether it keeps making every reasonable effort, the tool does not know.
- The rent you paid. The statute does not settle whether paying rent "with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)) waived this. If the nightly drops are a continuing noncompliance, paying does not waive it. On the other reading, paying with that knowledge waived it, and only a new or different failure starts over.

What to send, and how. Your lease allows a notice to the landlord only by hand to the leasing office, by certified mail to its address, or by e-mail to the office address (Lease Section 13.1). Your portal reports are not among these, and your lease says a maintenance request "is not by itself a notice under Section 13.1" (Lease Section 7.2). The statute lists delivery by "mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(4)). E-mail under 83.505 needs a signed addendum agreeing to it (Fla. Stat. 83.505(1)), and the tool does not know whether you signed one.

What it must say. A letter that only asks for a credit does not start either 7-day period. To be the notice that lets you end the lease, it must be one "specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)). To be the notice for the not-paying-rent defense, it must be one "specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant not to pay rent by reason thereof" (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)). Your three portal reports said neither.

When. The program's deadlines show nothing computed yet, because the facts are not all confirmed: the sheet still asks whether your lease says the landlord must repair this kind of problem. Each 7-day period runs from the delivery of such a notice. You have not delivered one, so neither has started.

If you only want the credit, you do not have to send either 7-day notice. A letter that only asks is a request, and it does not start either 7-day period. Your lease says no interruption entitles you to "any reduction or abatement of Rent" (Lease Section 5.2), and a term like that is void to the extent it waives a part II remedy (Fla. Stat. 83.47(1)(a)). Whether a part II rent reduction applies to you is the not-known-yet point set out above.

The sheet's question is whether your lease says the landlord must repair this kind of problem, for example in a clause on maintenance or repairs. Only you can answer it, and the tool does not assume either way. Here is what the lease says nearby. The repairs clause lists "the heating, air-conditioning, plumbing, and electrical systems serving the Unit and the appliances Landlord furnishes" (Lease Section 7.1); internet is not named in those words. Rent includes "high-speed internet (Wi-Fi)" (Lease Section 5.1), and the landlord is not liable for outages "caused by a provider" (Lease Section 5.2). Whether any of that is a promise to repair the Wi-Fi is your reading to give. If you answer yes, ending the lease turns next on the rent-waiver point, which the statute does not settle. If you answer no, it turns on a local housing code. Your answer does not decide whether you can ask for a credit.

Before I draft the letter I need three things. First, how many days you want to give them to reply. Second, how you will send it. Your lease says: "Every notice from Resident to Landlord under this Lease or Florida law must be in writing and delivered by hand to the leasing office at 2600 SW Hartwell Lane, Gainesville, Florida 32608, sent by certified mail to that address, or sent by e-mail to office@magnoliarow.example." (Lease Section 13.1). Third, which kind of letter:
- preserve: "Describes the condition and asks for the repair. Cites nothing."
- assert: "Adds the 83.51(1) duty, quoted." The letter would quote the sentence of 83.51(1) that begins "The landlord at all times during the tenancy shall". That section covers codes, structure, and plumbing. You confirmed this problem is not the structure or plumbing, and the code point is not known yet.
- escalate: "Adds the 83.56(1) sentence, quoted." The letter would quote the sentence of 83.56(1) on ending the lease after 7 days.
Which one?

content: The letter appears above; tell me if you want changes.

On the letter: I cannot fix those two lines from here. The letter is built from the sheet, and a confirmed answer changes only through the sheet. "Problem started" prints the start date on your sheet, which is the pool date, and "Written notice date" prints the date of your first portal report. You are right that a portal request is not by itself a notice under your lease (Lease Section 7.2). This letter is a request, not the notice in 83.56(1) or 83.60(1)(b), as the program's note under it says. If the Wi-Fi drops began on a different date, tell me that date and I will suggest it to the sheet, which then asks you to confirm it.

On acting together: it is not just you, but each path has limits.

Retaliation. A landlord may not retaliate by raising rent discriminatorily, cutting services, or bringing a possession or other civil action, where the tenant "has organized, encouraged, or participated in a tenant organization" (Fla. Stat. 83.64(1)(b)). The tenant "must have acted in good faith" (Fla. Stat. 83.64(1)). The statute text does not say whether a petition signed by about 40 tenants is a tenant organization, and you said it in chat but have not confirmed it on the sheet. The protection also "does not apply" where the landlord proves good cause, and good cause includes "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" (Fla. Stat. 83.64(3)). Salmonte v. Eilertson, 526 So. 2d 179, read 83.64(3) and held the retaliation defense could not be raised by a tenant who admitted breaching the lease, because good cause included "violation of the rental agreement" (at 180). That tenant admitted unauthorized pets and other violations, and nothing you confirmed is a breach, so the case does not match you. It would cut against any tenant in your group who breaches the lease.

A joint suit. Whether tenants can sue together as a class is not an option the tool tracks, and whether a court would allow it is not settled. K.D. Lewis Enterprises Corp. v. Smith, 445 So. 2d 1032, read the 1981 statute. Tenants who complained the landlord did not maintain their apartments asked to represent all tenants in the complex, and the court held the trial court "correctly refused to permit the tenants to appear as representatives of a class" (at 1034), because the effect "would unquestionably vary from apartment to apartment and from tenant to tenant" (at 1034). That cuts against you where your losses differ, as the gym, study rooms, and Wi-Fi may from one tenant to the next. A later case, First Hanover v. Vazquez, follows it. Olen Properties Corp. v. Moss, 981 So. 2d 515, went the other way: tenants all charged the same kind of fee, and the court found "commonality and typicality among the proposed members of the class" (at 520). That fits better where every tenant paid the same $150 fee. But the tenants there argued the fee broke Chapter 83, and the tool found no section of part II that gives a refund of an amenity fee. A dissent in Olen would not have allowed the class to proceed (at 521).

Each tenant's own rights. The notices that let a tenant end the lease or defend against a possession case must be "written notice by the tenant" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)), so each tenant's rights turn on that tenant's own lease, facts, and notice. The tool found nothing in your lease's text under "class", "arbitration", or "tenant association".
